entities.name: Classic of Poetry
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Collection of Chinese poetry, comprising works dating from the 11th to 7th centuries BC Created by various authors. Dating to c. 700 BCE.

The Classic of Poetry is one of China's four great classics and a cornerstone of Confucian literature. It was compiled during the Zhou Dynasty (1046–256 BCE) by scholars who gathered and edited the works of earlier poets, such as the legendary poet Wen Yao (c. 1200 BCE). The collection contains over 300 poems, many of which were written on ancient oracle bones or other artifacts.

The Classic of Poetry has had a profound impact on Chinese literature and culture, influencing generations of poets and thinkers. Its themes of love, nature, and morality continue to resonate with readers today. The poem 'Li Sao' (also known as the 'Ode to the River'), which laments the decline of the Han Dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE), is still widely studied and admired.

The Classic of Poetry has been translated into many languages and has inspired countless adaptations, including films, plays, and musical compositions. Its influence can be seen in Japanese literature, particularly in the works of Matsuo Bashō (1644–1694 CE).

Despite its ancient origins, the Classic of Poetry remains a vital part of Chinese cultural heritage, offering insights into the country's rich history, philosophy, and artistic traditions.

The most famous line from the Classic of Poetry is 'Spring cannot be controlled; / Autumn cannot be stopped.' (Chu Fu, 'Ode to Spring'), which captures the timeless essence of poetry.

In 2016, a team of Chinese researchers discovered that the earliest surviving copies of the Classic of Poetry date back to around 500 BCE.
